abstract: Introduction The VeriStrat® test (VS) is a blood-based assay that predicts a patient's response to therapy by analyzing eight features in a spectrum obtained from matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight (MALDI-TOF) analysis of human serum and plasma. In a recent analysis of the INSIGHT clinical trial ( NCT03289780 ), it was found that the VS labels, VS Good and VS Poor, can effectively predict the responsiveness of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients to immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapy. However, while VS measures the intensities of spectral features using MALDI-TOF analysis, the specific proteoforms underlying these features have not been comprehensively identified. Objectives The objective of this study was to identify the proteoforms that are measured by VS. Methods To resolve the features obtained from the low-resolution MALDI-TOF procedure used to acquire mass spectra for VS DeepMALDI® analysis of serum was employed. This technique allowed for the identification of finer peaks within these features. Additionally, a combination of reversed-phase fractionation and liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) was then used to identify the proteoforms associated with these peaks. Results The analysis revealed that the primary constituents of the spectrum measured by VS are serum amyloid A1, serum amyloid A2, serum amyloid A4, C-reactive protein, and beta-2 microglobulin. Conclusion Proteoforms involved in host immunity were identified as significant components of these features. This newly acquired information improves our understanding of how VS can accurately predict patient response to therapy. It opens up additional studies that can expand our understanding even further.

Material and methods
2.1
Samples
De-identified, serum samples from human subjects diagnosed with lung cancer were acquired from commercial biobanks under their consent protocols [Discovery Life Sciences (Huntsville, AL), ProMedDx (Norton, MA), ProteoGenex (Inglewood, CA) and BioIVT (Westbury, NY)]. Additional archived, de-identified samples were from patients consented into the Biodesix-sponsored PROSE study
[11]
(Randomized Proteomic Stratified Phase III Study of Second-Line Erlotinib versus Chemotherapy in Patients With Inoperable Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer,
NCT00989690
).
Of 53 serum samples acquired from the biobanks, 26 serum samples with VS Good status and 16 serum samples with VS Poor status were combined to create large pools of VS Good and VS Poor serum, respectively. The pooled samples are referred to as VSP and VSG hereafter. The pooled samples were used for top-down mass spectrometry analysis and immunodepletion of serum amyloid A and C-reactive protein. Two additional samples with VS Good and VS Poor status, called VS Good and VS Poor, were not included in the VSG and VSP pools.
2.2
Reagents
Antibodies: Biotin-conjugated mouse monoclonal anti-human antibody to serum amyloid A (SAA; Cat. No. MO-C40028TB) and C-reactive protein (CRP; Cat. No. MAB5101) were purchased from Anogen (Mississauga, ON, Canada,) and VWR International (Radnor, PA), respectively.
Solvents and other materials: Acetonitrile, HPLC grade water, and trifluoroacetic acid were purchased from VWR International (Radnor, PA). Phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) and Dynabeads™ M-280 streptavidin were purchased from ThermoFisher Scientific (Carlsbad, CA). Bondapak® C18 bulk packing material (125 Å pore size, 37–55 µm particle diameter) was purchased from Waters (Milford, MA). Sinapinic acid was purchased from Proteochem (Loves Park, IL). Serum cards were purchased from GE HealthCare (Buckinghamshire, UK). PBS with 0.05 % Tween® 20 (PBST) was purchased from Millipore Sigma (Burlington, MA). Protein Calibration Standard I was purchased from Bruker (Billerica, MA).
2.3
VS spectral acquisition
VS spectra were acquired on a microflex® MALDI-TOF mass spectrometer (Bruker, Billerica, MA) equipped with a 337 nm nitrogen laser with a maximum repetition rate of 60 Hz. The instrument was operated in positive-ion, linear mode, scanning a mass range of
m
/
z
3000 to 30,000 Da. 500 shot spectra (in 25 shot steps) were acquired from three replicate spots per sample after external calibration of the instrument with a mixture of calibrants in Protein Calibration Standard I.
Serum samples were prepared for VS spectra acquisition as follows. Samples were thawed and 10 μL aliquots of each sample were spotted onto serum cards. The cards were allowed to dry for 1 h at ambient temperature, after which one 3 mm punch was excised from the serum spot. The punch was placed in a 1.5 mL tube, to which 50 µL of water was added then vortexed gently for 3 min. Twenty microliters of the serum extract were transferred to a 0.5 mL tube. Twenty microliters of matrix (25 mg of sinapinic acid per 1 mL of 50 % acetonitrile:50 % water plus 0.1 % trifluoroacetic acid; percentages are volume/volume) were added to 20 µL of serum extract and mixed by vortexing. Finally, three aliquots of 2 µL sample:matrix mix were spotted onto a MALDI target (Hudson Surface Technology, Closter, NJ), which was allowed to dry on the bench before placement in the MALDI mass spectrometer.
VS spectra were analyzed according to the standard protocols used in clinical specimen testing for VeriStrat.
2.4
DeepMALDI spectral acquisition
DeepMALDI
[2]
spectra were acquired on a rapifleX® MALDI-TOF mass spectrometer (Bruker, Billerica, MA) equipped with a Bruker smartbeam™ laser. The instrument was operated in positive-ion, linear mode, scanning a mass range of
m
/
z
3000 to 30,000 Da. External calibration was performed using peaks
m
/
z
= 3320.0000, 4158.7338, 6636.7971, 9429.3020, 13,890.4398, 15,877.5801, and 28,093.9510 or Bruker’s Protein Calibration Standard I, consisting of a mixture of insulin, ubiquitin I, cytochrome C and myoglobin.
Serum samples were prepared for DeepMALDI analysis as follows. Samples were thawed and 3 μL aliquots of each sample were spotted onto serum cards, which were allowed to dry for 1 h at ambient temperature. The whole serum spot was punched out with a 6 mm skin biopsy punch, placed in a centrifugal filter with 0.45 µm nylon membrane, and 100 μL of HPLC grade water was added. The punch was vortexed gently for 10 min, then spun down at 14,000 rcf for 2 min. The flow-through was removed and transferred back onto the punch for a second round of extraction. Twenty microliters of the filtrate from each sample were transferred to a 0.5 mL microcentrifuge tube for MALDI analysis. All subsequent sample preparation steps were conducted in a custom-designed humidity and temperature control chamber (Coy Lab Products, Grass Lake, MI), set to 30 °C and 10 % relative humidity.
An equal volume of freshly prepared matrix (25 mg of sinapinic acid per 1 mL of 50 % acetonitrile:50 % water plus 0.1 % trifluoroacetic acid) was added to each 20 µL serum extract and the mix was vortexed for 30 s. The first five aliquots (5 × 2 µL) of sample:matrix mix were discarded. Eight aliquots of 2 µL sample:matrix mix were spotted onto a stainless steel MALDI target plate (Bruker, Billerica, MA).
For immunodepletion experiments, the reconstituted eluents from the immunodepleted serum samples were mixed with an equal volume of matrix solution (25 mg of sinapinic acid per 1 mL of 50 % acetonitrile:50 % water plus 0.1 % trifluoroacetic acid) and spotted onto stainless steel MALDI plates for spectra acquisition on the Bruker rapifleX.
The MALDI target was allowed to dry in the environmental control chamber before placement in the MALDI mass spectrometer.
DeepMALDI spectra were analyzed using Biodesix-developed software developed to deal with the large dynamic range observed in serum
[21]
. For quantitative analysis of the spectra in the PROSE set, only the strongly background-subtracted peak structure denoted as ‘FINE’ in
[21]
was used. This mitigates tails of large peaks from contributing to the intensity of smaller neighboring peaks. Proper normalization is essential when comparing peak intensities in MALDI spectra across samples, such as in the correlation analysis performed below. After background subtraction, peak intensities were normalized across samples using the intensity of peaks with the smallest variation across samples (as determined by an iterative process). Peaks used for normalization were at

/

: 3433, 3556, 3564, 3684, 3711, 3782, 3831, 4017, 4578, 4604, 4693, 5116, 5415, 6206, 6541, 7054, 7064, 8255, 9724, 9737, 14039, 14054, 14070, 14101, 14118, 14141, 14159, 14178, 14261, 14273, 14395 and 28102.

Calibration of MALDI-TOF

/

To ensure mass accuracy of DeepMALDI spectra, the Bruker rapifleX was calibrated using Protein Calibration Standard I (Bruker, Billerica, MA) – a mixture of insulin, ubiquitin I, cytochrome C, and myoglobin – and reference spectra were acquired. The
m
/

axis of all DeepMALDI spectra were aligned to these reference spectra. Accuracy of the aligned
m
/

axes were confirmed by evaluating the peaks corresponding to known proteoforms within the
m
/

range of the calibration standard but located outside of VS features.
2.6
Preparation of samples for top-down proteomics
To prepare serum samples for top-down proteomics analysis, 50 µL of serum was diluted with 50 µL of water and filtered through a 0.2 µm modified nylon filter to remove particulates. Twenty microliters of the filtered sample were fractionated on a high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) system with a C4 column (Waters XBridge Protein BEH, 2.1 mm × 250 mm, 300 Å pore size, 3.5 µm particle size). Proteins were separated at ambient temperature with a flow rate of 0.2 mL/min using a linear gradient from 44 % B to 60 % B over 60 min (solvent A: 0.1 % trifluoroacetic acid in water; solvent B: 0.1 % trifluoroacetic acid in 90 % acetonitrile–water). Twenty 0.6 mL fractions were collected over the course of the gradient. The fractions were completely dried using a centrifugal vacuum concentrator. To reduce disulfide bridges, the dried samples were reconstituted in liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry-grade water containing 20 mM tris(2-carboxyethyl) phosphine and incubated for 1 h at ambient temperature with constant vortexing.
2.7
Top-down analysis of proteins by mass spectrometry
Analyses were performed using a Bruker nanoElute (two-column method, Bruker TEN C18 column, 500 nL/min flow rate, 40 °C) The instrument was coupled with a Bruker timsTOF fleX mass spectrometer using the captive-spray source. Initially, samples were run in MS1-only mode, with the TIMS disabled and a spectra rate of 1 Hz within a mass range of 100–1700
m
/
z
. The data obtained from the Bruker software was exported in ASCII format. Subsequently, a custom MATLAB script was utilized to deconvolute the spectra and select precursors for fragmentation. In the next step, samples were run again in auto-MS/MS mode with the selected precursors added to the scheduled precursor list. The experiment was conducted with the TIMS disabled, a 1 Hz MS spectra rate, a 5 Hz MS/MS spectra rate, and a mass range of 100–1700
m
/
z
. Active exclusion was disabled, an isolation width of 2 was employed, and collision energies ranged from 25 to 65 eV, based on mass and charge state.
2.8
Analysis of top-down proteomics data
Raw tandem mass spectrometry data were exported from the Bruker software in ASCII format. The spectra were deconvoluted and searched using custom MATLAB scripts developed in-house. An extensive proteoform database was created using neXtProt
[22]
SPARQL queries. The database included all human protein entries within the SwissProt database with a molecular weight of ≤35 kDa (since DeepMALDI spectra were acquired in the range of 3,000–30,000
m
/
z
). For each of these proteins, all allelic variants (with a frequency greater than 1 %) and mature forms (e.g., signal- and pro-peptides removed) were also included. Truncations of up to three residues from either terminus were considered, as well as the following chemical modifications: water and ammonia loss, oxidation, hydroxylation, acetylation, succinylation, amidation, and specific glycosylations documented within the neXtProt database. Both MS and MS/MS data were utilized during matching, and scores for individual fragment ion matches were weighted based on the similarity between observed and predicted isotope distributions. Matches were confirmed by visual inspection of the spectra. Identified proteoforms were then mapped to the DeepMALDI spectra by comparing their calculated masses to the
m
/
z
values of the DeepMALDI peaks.
2.9
Immunodepletion of serum amyloid A (SAA) and C-reactive protein (CRP) from serum
Three microliters of VSP were diluted with 277 µL of PBS. Then, twenty microliters of biotin-conjugated monoclonal mouse anti-human SAA antibody were added to the diluted serum and incubated at room temperature for two hours. During the two-hour incubation period, 100 µL of streptavidin modified magnetic particles (Dynabeads™ M-280 Streptavidin) were washed three times with a series of 900 µL, 100 µL, and 100 µL of PBST. Afterward, the diluted VSP and antibody mix were added to the washed Dynabeads and incubated for 30 min at room temperature. The antigen–antibody complex-coated Dynabeads were then separated from the solution using the DynaMag™ -2 magnet (Thermo, Carlsbad, CA), and the resulting supernatant was transferred to a new tube. Subsequently, the supernatant from the antigen–antibody complex was mixed with 10 µL of biotin-conjugated anti-SAA antibody and 100 µL of washed Dynabeads for a second round of SAA depletion following the same procedure described above. Ninety microliters out of the 300 µL of supernatant from the second round of depletion were transferred to a new tube for C18 clean-up and DeepMALDI analysis.
To deplete CRP from VSP, the same procedure used for SAA depletion was followed with some changes: instead of adding biotin-conjugated monoclonal mouse anti-human SAA antibody to the diluted serum, 10 µL of biotin-conjugated monoclonal mouse anti-human CRP antibody were added. Additionally, the second round of depletion was omitted.
Negative controls for both SAA and CRP depletions were performed in parallel, following the exact same steps, but without the addition of the anti-SAA and anti-CRP antibodies.
2.10
C18 cleanup of immunodepleted serum
C18 cleanup was performed on the samples to eliminate contaminants, such as salts, that may have been introduced during immunodepletion and could interfere with MALDI spectra acquisition. The C18 particles were activated using a mixture of 50 % acetonitrile and 50 % water, and then equilibrated with a solution containing 0.5 % trifluoroacetic acid in 5 % acetonitrile. The immunodepleted serum and the supernatant from corresponding controls (without antibody) were adjusted to a final concentration of 0.5 % trifluoroacetic acid and 5 % acetonitrile, and mixed with the activated C18 particles in a spin filter tube. Centrifugation was used to isolate the unbound material. The flow-through obtained from centrifugation was added back to the C18 particles for further binding. After another round of centrifugation, the C18 particles were washed with an aqueous solution containing 0.5 % trifluoroacetic acid in 5 % acetonitrile. The serum proteins bound to the C18 particles were eluted with two 20-µL aliquots of 70 % acetonitrile in water. The eluents were combined, and the solvent was removed using a centrifugal vacuum concentrator. The dried eluents were then reconstituted in 20 µL of reagent grade water.
2.11
Ethics statement
All samples were collected under ethics-approved protocols according to Institutional Review Board/Independent Ethics Committee requirements of the respective biobanks and the PROSE study (
NCT00989690
). As only fully anonymized patient samples were used that were not obtained specifically for use in this study through an interaction or intervention with living individuals, neither additional informed consent nor IRB review were required.

Introduction
The VeriStrat (VS) test is a proteomic assay that utilizes mass spectrometry and is performed on human serum and plasma samples. Detailed information regarding the development and initial validation of the test has been previously published
[1]
,
[2]
,
[3]
. In summary, triplicate mass spectra are obtained from the patient samples using matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization (MALDI) time-of-flight (TOF) mass spectrometry. To standardize the spectra for accurate comparison between samples, several data processing steps are performed, including background subtraction, alignment, and normalization. The processed spectra are then evaluated by assessing the area under the curves within eight specific mass spectral regions. The definitions of these eight spectral features, referred to as VS1-VS8, are provided in
Table 1
.

The values of these eight mass spectral features are compared with those of the samples in the classification-labelled reference set using a seven-nearest neighbor algorithm to determine whether each spectrum is classified as “VS Good” or “VS Poor”. If the three replicate spectra generated from a sample produce consistent results, i.e., all “VS Good” or all “VS Poor”, that result is reported as the VS classification. If the replicate results are inconsistent, an “Indeterminate” classification is assigned. In the INSIGHT study (
NCT03289780
), only 40 out of 2376 samples (<2%) received an indeterminate result
[1]
. Spectral quality is ensured through multiple quality control checks. For instance, the spectra must contain a minimum number of detectable peaks, the noise level must not exceed a predetermined limit, and a minimum number of peaks must be used during spectral alignment. The spectra are also monitored to prevent a VS Poor result from being generated due to the presence of a large interfering peak at
m
/
z
= 11.7 kDa, which is rarely observed except in patients with severely compromised liver function due to extremely high levels of beta-2 microglobulin (B2M)
[4]
,
[5]
.
The abundances of multiple serum proteins are correlated with VS classification, including C-reactive protein (CRP), interleukin-6 (IL-6), serum amyloid A (SAA), the cytokeratin 19 fragment CYFRA 21-1, insulin-like growth factor 2 (IGF-2), and osteopontin
[6]
. Set enrichment analysis techniques have shown that VS classification is associated with acute phase response
[6]
,
[7]
,
[8]
, acute inflammatory response, and complement activation
[7]
,
[8]
. It is well known that truncated proteoforms of serum amyloid A are present in the mass/charge range of some of the VS features in
Table 1
[9]
,
[10]
.
The VS test has demonstrated both prognostic and predictive power in the advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) setting and in other tumor types. A prospective, randomized clinical trial showed that the test can predict differential benefit from erlotinib versus single-agent chemotherapy between patients with advanced NSCLC assigned a VS Poor or VS Good classification of pretreatment serum
[11]
. Individual studies and
meta
-analyses have shown that patients assigned a pretreatment VS Good classification have significantly better outcomes than those assigned a VS Poor classification across multiple treatment regimens and in the absence of active therapy in the advanced NSCLC setting
[12]
,
[13]
,
[14]
,
[15]
.
Most recently, the VS test has shown potential as a prognostic marker for immunotherapy treatment of advanced NSCLC
[1]
,
[16]
,
[17]
, as well as predicting which patients may benefit most from the addition of chemotherapy to immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI)
[1]
. The prognostic power of the test has also been identified in other advanced solid tumors, including colorectal cancer, squamous cell cancer of the head and neck
[18]
, pancreatic cancer
[19]
, and breast cancer
[20]
.
The aim of the current study was to definitively determine the protein components of the VS features. As a translational goal, the study aimed to understand the potential role of these proteins in immuno-oncology. Additionally, the study explored why the presence of these proteins detected in VS could influence its ability to predict outcomes of NSCLC immunotherapy.

2.9
Immunodepletion of serum amyloid A (SAA) and C-reactive protein (CRP) from serum
Three microliters of VSP were diluted with 277 µL of PBS. Then, twenty microliters of biotin-conjugated monoclonal mouse anti-human SAA antibody were added to the diluted serum and incubated at room temperature for two hours. During the two-hour incubation period, 100 µL of streptavidin modified magnetic particles (Dynabeads™ M-280 Streptavidin) were washed three times with a series of 900 µL, 100 µL, and 100 µL of PBST. Afterward, the diluted VSP and antibody mix were added to the washed Dynabeads and incubated for 30 min at room temperature. The antigen–antibody complex-coated Dynabeads were then separated from the solution using the DynaMag™ -2 magnet (Thermo, Carlsbad, CA), and the resulting supernatant was transferred to a new tube. Subsequently, the supernatant from the antigen–antibody complex was mixed with 10 µL of biotin-conjugated anti-SAA antibody and 100 µL of washed Dynabeads for a second round of SAA depletion following the same procedure described above. Ninety microliters out of the 300 µL of supernatant from the second round of depletion were transferred to a new tube for C18 clean-up and DeepMALDI analysis.
To deplete CRP from VSP, the same procedure used for SAA depletion was followed with some changes: instead of adding biotin-conjugated monoclonal mouse anti-human SAA antibody to the diluted serum, 10 µL of biotin-conjugated monoclonal mouse anti-human CRP antibody were added. Additionally, the second round of depletion was omitted.
Negative controls for both SAA and CRP depletions were performed in parallel, following the exact same steps, but without the addition of the anti-SAA and anti-CRP antibodies.
2.10
C18 cleanup of immunodepleted serum
C18 cleanup was performed on the samples to eliminate contaminants, such as salts, that may have been introduced during immunodepletion and could interfere with MALDI spectra acquisition. The C18 particles were activated using a mixture of 50 % acetonitrile and 50 % water, and then equilibrated with a solution containing 0.5 % trifluoroacetic acid in 5 % acetonitrile. The immunodepleted serum and the supernatant from corresponding controls (without antibody) were adjusted to a final concentration of 0.5 % trifluoroacetic acid and 5 % acetonitrile, and mixed with the activated C18 particles in a spin filter tube. Centrifugation was used to isolate the unbound material. The flow-through obtained from centrifugation was added back to the C18 particles for further binding. After another round of centrifugation, the C18 particles were washed with an aqueous solution containing 0.5 % trifluoroacetic acid in 5 % acetonitrile. The serum proteins bound to the C18 particles were eluted with two 20-µL aliquots of 70 % acetonitrile in water. The eluents were combined, and the solvent was removed using a centrifugal vacuum concentrator. The dried eluents were then reconstituted in 20 µL of reagent grade water.
2.11
Ethics statement
All samples were collected under ethics-approved protocols according to Institutional Review Board/Independent Ethics Committee requirements of the respective biobanks and the PROSE study (
NCT00989690
). As only fully anonymized patient samples were used that were not obtained specifically for use in this study through an interaction or intervention with living individuals, neither additional informed consent nor IRB review were required.

The development of the VS algorithm
[3]

[2]

In the DeepMALDI spectra, we observed 81 distinct peaks within the previously defined eight VS feature ranges. A listing of these peaks and their assignments to VS features is provided in
Supplementary Table S1
. To gain a more comprehensive understanding of the biological basis of the VeriStrat test, we aimed to identify the specific proteoforms that constitute the VS features.
In a standard bottom-up proteomics approach, complex protein mixtures, such as serum, undergo digestion with a protease, typically trypsin, before being analyzed using tandem mass spectrometry. Tandem mass spectra are utilized to determine the peptides present in the digested mixture, enabling inference of the protein groups found in the original sample. However, this method can compromise proteoform-level information. To address this limitation and identify specific proteoforms within serum samples, we employed top-down proteomics
[24]
. This involved introducing whole proteoforms (without digestion) onto the mass spectrometer for tandem mass spectrometric analysis via liquid chromatography and electrospray ionization (ESI).
Focusing on the predominant peaks in the VS spectra, we identified 44 proteoforms, which constitute the major contribution to the values of the eight VS features. These are listed in

[5]

[30]

[9]
,

The association of inflammatory markers, particularly SAA and CRP, with VS classification has also been reported previously
[6]
,
[33]
. The association of SAA4 with VS features VS7 and VS8 is a novel discovery to our knowledge.
Confirming and extending upon a previous report
[10]
, our use of top-down identification allowed for a direct assignment of different SAA alleles to different VS features. It is interesting to note that we observed the less common allele SAA2.2, with an allele frequency of 0.140067, together with the more common allele SAA2.1, with an allele frequency of 0.83539
[34]
, in a single patient’s sample (see
Fig. 1
A/B).
DeepMALDI peaks in the lower mass range of the VS feature VS1 are doubly-charged peaks of the proteoforms in the higher mass VS features VS2–VS6, as the pattern of peaks is identical, and the peak positions match nearly perfectly.
Additionally, in the DeepMALDI analysis, we observed a well-defined peak at 11,514 Da, which was more visible in VS Good samples and absent in the doubly-charged VS1 range (see
Fig. 2
). This peak had a high Pearson correlation (0.92) with a peak at 23,025 Da in the PROSE set, which was assigned from the literature

[23]

[35]

The top-down procedure allowed for excellent coverage of the protein fragments in the respective MS2 spectra, enabling detailed identification of the observed proteoform.
Supplementary Figs. S1–S3
illustrate examples of this matching procedure and demonstrate the high quality of matches on both the MS1 and MS2 levels for SAA4-desKY, B2M, and SAA1.1.
To confirm top-down identifications using an orthogonal approach, we conducted selected depletion experiments. In
Fig. 3
A and 3B, we present the reduction in SAA peaks resulting from depletion with an anti-SAA antibody. While nearly all SAA peaks were reduced, it appears that the antibody used exhibited greater efficacy in binding to SAA1 than SAA2 (e.g., the reduction in the SAA1.1 peak is much more pronounced compared to that in the SAA2.1 peak). Moreover, there was no significant reduction in SAA4 proteoforms, indicating specificity towards the SAA1 and SAA2 isoforms. The decrease in peak height resulting from SAA immunodepletion also confirmed the assignment of peaks originating from adducts. Depletion strongly affected peaks such as SAA1.1 + matrix, SAA1.1 + Na, and SAA1.1desR + Na. As expected, the CRP(z = 2) peak remained unaffected by this depletion process.
3.2
Correlation analysis of identified proteoforms
The association of inflammatory proteins, specifically SAA, with VS classification has been extensively investigated in previous studies
[6]
,
[33]
. In this study, we build upon this research by demonstrating the association between the identified DeepMALDI peaks and VS classifications. We also explore the correlations between these peaks using the available samples from the PROSE study
[11]
as our dataset.
Fig. 4
A presents a heatmap displaying the intensities of a subset (fewer adducts) of the identified DeepMALDI peaks across individual VS Good and VS Poor samples. With the exception of the SAA4-desKY peaks, all other identified peaks exhibited a significant association with VS result (Mann-Whitney p < 0.001; refer to
supplementary Fig. S4
). However, determining a single cut-off value for each peak is challenging due to the continuum of values observed for each feature and the overlap between VS groups in the low peak intensity range. This lack of simple cut-offs is not surprising considering that the VS test is multivariate in nature, with VS classification determined through a k-nearest neighbor (kNN) algorithm utilizing a reference set comprising 26 samples
[3]
.

4
Discussion
The blood-based VeriStrat proteomic test is based on eight MALDI-TOF spectral features spanning an
m
/
z
range of 5811 to 12658. However, as this test relies on Biodesix’s early generation MALDI-TOF technologies, each individual spectral feature is broad and believed to encompass multiple proteins and their proteoforms
[6]
,
[9]
,
[10]
. In the latest iteration of DeepMALDI proteomics (circa 2021), the fine structure spectrum underlying each of the eight VS features was discovered to be composed of 81 underlying protein peaks. Through a combination of top-down proteomics and mass inferences, the proteoforms responsible for 44 of these peaks were identified, with immunodepletion used to validate many of these findings. These 44 spectral peaks primarily consist of CRP and B2M, as well as different proteoforms of SAA1, SAA2, and SAA4.
The VeriStrat proteomic test has recently been demonstrated in the INSIGHT clinical trial
[1]
and by Chae et al.
[16]
to be capable of identifying patients with non-small cell lung cancer who are most likely to respond to ICIs. There are indications that this test may also be useful in determining which patients would benefit most from adding platinum doublet chemotherapy to ICI therapy. One objective of this present study was to definitively identify the VS proteins in order to gain a better understanding of their role in cancer immunobiology and use them as relevant biomarkers for response to ICI treatments.
Several studies have individually examined SAA, CRP, and B2M as univariate biomarkers and potential prognostic or predictive biomarkers for various cancer outcomes
[36]
,
[37]
,
[38]
,
[39]
,
[40]
,
[41]
,
[42]
. Other research has explored these proteins as potential predictive biomarkers for outcomes following ICI therapy in different types of cancers such as lung, breast, colon, melanoma, and others
[37]
,
[39]
,
[40]
,
[42]
,
[43]
. However, none of these studies have resulted in the use of these proteins as individual clinical biomarkers for cancer. This is likely due to the challenges inherent in applying univariate analyses to covariance and correlation in complex biological systems, as well as using small non-representative patient cohorts for biomarker discovery
[44]
,
[45]
,
[46]
,
[47]
. For example, a review and
meta
-analysis of CRP found that among 33 studies, 19 different cutoff levels were identified for CRP to be prognostic of ICI outcomes
[48]
. Our findings align with this, as we observed considerable overlap between the abundance of these markers at the decision margin of the VS test, making it difficult to establish a simple threshold.
On the other hand, multivariate tests address the limitations of univariate tests by measuring multiple features related to an outcome
[49]
,
[50]
. The VeriStrat test utilizes multivariate analysis by incorporating SAA isoforms, CRP, and B2M into a single test that has been validated in both prognostic and predictive settings for NSCLC outcomes
[36]
,
[37]
,
[38]
,
[39]
,
[40]
,
[41]
,
[42]
.
Recently, the VeriStrat test has demonstrated its ability to stratify outcomes (VS groups) for patients receiving single agent immunotherapy and triplet therapy
[1]
, with point-estimates showing differential outcomes. This finding raises the question: How are the proteins measured by the VeriStrat test related to immunotherapy outcomes from a prognostic and biologic perspective?
SAA proteins exhibit up to a 1000-fold increase in expression during the acute phase response, which occurs after an immune response or tissue insult as part of an attempt to restore homeostasis
[51]
. SAA is prognostic of outcomes in NSCLC and other cancers
[36]
,
[37]
,
[39]
, as well as efficacy and outcomes of ICI therapy
[52]
,
[53]
. It is important to note that it is not yet determined how individual SAA proteins and their proteoforms contribute to prognosis or prediction. SAA has been shown to activate myeloid-derived suppressor cells that inhibit the immune system
[54]
,
[55]
. Therefore, increased SAA levels may directly impact ICI efficacy by suppressing the immune system even when PD1/PD-L1 is inhibited.
CRP is considered a prototypical acute phase reactant protein
[56]
that exhibits increased expression during inflammation and tissue damage
[57]
. It serves as a recognized biomarker of inflammation
[58]
,
[59]
and is routinely used as a clinical biomarker for overall immune system activity. Several studies have demonstrated the potential of CRP as a prognostic factor for ICI therapy outcomes in various cancers
[48]
. However, a definitive cutoff level for CRP has not yet been established to make it clinically useful in the context of ICI therapy. Interestingly, CRP may play an active role in dampening the adaptive immune system
[60]
, suggesting that it may suppress the immune system even when PD1/PD-L1 is inhibited.
B2M is crucial for antigen presentation, including potential tumor antigens, by tumor cells in the context of the major histocompatibility complex class 1 (MHC I)
[61]
,
[62]
. B2M is required for loading antigens into MHC I. Cytotoxic CD8+ T cells recognize MHC I-bound antigen on cell surfaces, and B2M plays a critical role in CD8+ binding to and lysis/killing of tumor cells
[63]
. Elevated levels of B2M in blood have been associated with an increased risk of cancer development, including NSCLC, as shown in the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities (ARIC) study
[64]
,
[65]
, and are elevated in different cancers
[66]
,
[67]
. Different levels of B2M have been shown to be prognostic factors for outcomes in various cancers
[68]
,
[69]
,
[70]
,
[71]
. Additionally, B2M has been found to correlate with ICI therapeutic response in NSCLC and melanoma
[72]
,
[73]
, likely due to its impact on tumor antigen presentation disruption
[74]
.
As mentioned earlier, the VeriStrat proteomic test has recently demonstrated its ability to identify NSCLC patients who are most likely to respond to ICI therapy. There are indications that it may also provide insight into which patients would benefit most from adding platinum doublet therapy to ICI treatment
[1]
,
[16]
. In this context, we propose a model (
Fig. 5
) where the proteins measured by the VeriStrat proteomic test play active roles in the anti-tumor immune response. Increased levels of SAA and CRP are immunosuppressive, while varying levels of B2M expression likely influence tumor antigen presentation status. These immuno-oncology effects could explain why increased levels of SAA and CRP, as well as changes in B2M levels, contribute to the suppression of ICI activity and why the VeriStrat proteomic test is predictive of ICI treatment outcomes.
Fig. 5
Proposed immunomodulatory actions of SAA, CRP, and B2M in the context of the anti-tumor immune response.
A) Increased levels of CRP and SAA proteins have been shown to suppress the adaptive immune system. SAA activates MDSC, which suppresses T-cell activity. CRP has been shown to suppress both T-cell and B-cell activity. B) Normal cells express normal levels of B2M, which interacts with MHC class I to allow antigen loading and display on the cell surface to enable recognition by cytotoxic T cells. Cancer cells can silence expression of B2M through several mechanisms, resulting in a loss of MHC class I antigen presentation. Alternatively, cancer cells can export B2M to the extracellular space, preventing its interaction with MHC class I, again resulting in a loss of antigen presentation.
5
Conclusions
This study has identified B2M and CRP, as well as multiple proteoforms of SAA1, SAA2, and SAA4, as the main proteins measured by the VeriStrat proteomic test. These proteins have demonstrated prognostic value for different cancer outcomes and have active involvement in cancer immunobiology. This provides a potential mechanistic explanation for the VeriStrat proteomic test's capability to predict which patients may or may not benefit from adding chemotherapy to ICI treatment.
